previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for acute kidney injury with a creatinine rise from 1.1 to 5.0, attributed to cast nephropathy secondary to relapsed multiple myeloma. He was started on CyBorD chemotherapy and underwent three sessions of plasmapheresis, which led to improvement in renal function, with creatinine decreasing to 2.6 at discharge. He received continuous IV fluids and had a temporary pheresis line placed. His blood pressure was managed with uptitration of carvedilol and diltiazem and addition of doxazosin. Insulin was increased to 46 units of Lantus due to steroid-induced hyperglycemia. Oral vancomycin was continued on a taper for recurrent C. diff. He remained stable, avoided dialysis, and was discharged home with follow-up in oncology, nephrology, and endocrinology.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ y/o man with relapsed refractory IgA myeloma 
s/p autoSCT now on C2 CyBorD ___, T2DM, HTN, prostate CA, 
OSA, h/o PE who p/w dyspnea and abdominal bloating after recent 
admission for ___. 

INITIAL HOSPITAL COURSE ON OMED B ___ - ___:
- On arrival patient's clinical exam was most consistent with 
severe constipation. He had several large BMs overnight and 
reported subjective improvement in symptoms. Over the subsequent 
days his abdominal discomfort was intermittent and would improve 
with BMs. Because he did not fully improve and could not fully 
tolerate a regular diet we performed a CT of the abdomen which 
showed inflammation around the duodenum and stranding in the 
retroperitoneum. 
.
On ___ - he was NPO for large part of the day and had MRI of 
the abdomen that showed inflammation around the duodenum with 
stranding. He also had stranding in the retroperitoneum and 
pelvis. The mass next to the bladder noted to represent likely 
extramedullary hematopoiesis. 
.
On ___ he was hypoglycemic to 36 in the morning. This quickly 
resolved with D50 amp, glucose gel, and D10W IVF. He was 
encouraged to eat, which he did. Several hours later the 
patient's abdomen was noted to be significantly larger, and he 
was in significant pain, with guarding. Non peritoneal. Stat KUB 
showed 12cm marked distension of the abdomen. Given the acute 
change in clinical exam he was transferred to the ICU for 
further management. There was no evidence of pneumoperitoneum.
.
HOSPITAL COURSE IN ___ ___ - ___
He had an NGT placed for decompression. Given the concern for a 
possible duodenal mass that may be causing intermittent 
obstruction, GI was consulted. They recommended continued NG 
tube decompression. He initially had 4L of bilious residuals 
drained over the course of 24 hours but after 48 hours, his 
residuals decreased and he was successfully trialled on a diet. 
After reviewing MRI with radiology and GI, the duodenal mass was 
thought to be generalized inflammation from duodenitis. It was 
recommended that he be on a PPI. 

His FICU stay was complicated by persistent hypoglycemia 
requiring 48 hours of D10W gtt and Q1H fingersticks. Given his 
history of high long-acting insulin needs (taking 46U at night 
prior to hospitalization), he was given ___ dose his normal 
lantus dosing). Given his persistent hypoglycemia despite 
reduced insulin dosing, a C-peptide and insulin level were sent. 
The C-peptide was low and insulin level high, thought to be 
consistent with iatrogenic overdosing of insulin. Endocrine was 
consulted who felt that his insulin dosing at home was higher 
than baseline to account for his recent steroids and that his 
___ was contributing to delayed clearance of his insulin. They 
recommended holding his insulin and treating with sliding scale 
only as needed. With this regimen his hypoglycemia resolved. He 
was transferred back to the floor for further management on 
___. 
.

HOSPITAL COURSE ON HMED/OMED UPON TRANSFER OUT OF FICU BY 
PROBLEM (___):

ACUTE PROBLEMS:
-----------------
# Relapsed Refractory IgA Lambda Multiple Myeloma: The patient 
has a history of IgA MM, s/p prior auto-SCT and most recently on 
CyBorD C2D1 = ___. He was due for his next dose of velcade on 
admission. However, this was deferred given his acute abdominal 
symptoms. Following transfer out of the FICU, the patient was 
noted to have slowly downtrending counts (see pancytopenia) and 
as part of work-up, had repeat IgA, SPEP, and IFE consistent 
with relapse of Myleoma. He was given 4 days of dexamethasone 
40mg daily, followed by Cytoxan infusion x1. During this 
admission, he was continued on acyclovir and Bactrim (briefly 
switched to atovaquone given risk for myelosuppression) for 
prophylaxis, and given supportive blood transfusions PRN (4u 
pRBC and 3u Plts). He was also supplemented with folate and B12 
and set up with follow-up with Dr. ___ oncologist) 
shortly following discharge to discuss management of MM further.

# Pancytopenia: The patient, as detailed above, developed 
progressive anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia. 
Hemolysis, bleed, and vitamin deficiency were felt to be less 
likely. Overall, this was felt secondary to progressive multiple 
myeloma with marrow involvement. He was treated for his MM and 
low blood counts as above.

# Duodenitis of unclear etiology: The patient, as above, was 
diagnosed with duodenitis per MRCP in the context of severe 
abdominal distention, pain, and pseudoobstruction requiring NGT 
decompression. The etiology of his duodenitis was unclear, 
without clear infection as he improved despite only 1 day of abx 
therapy. One possible etiology would be velcade toxicity. He did 
undergo EGD, which also showed non-specific signs of duodenitis, 
with biopsies taken (pending at time of discharge). With 
supportive care on laxatives, the patient was moving his bowels 
regularly and without anymore abdominal pain or distention prior 
to discharge.

# Concern for Colonic Malignancy: The patient has a history of 
Strep Bovis and as above, presented with abdominal pain, 
distention, and constipation. As such, there was concern for 
possible colonic malignancy. Due to concern that with further 
cytotoxic therapy, the patient may become increasingly 
thrombocytopenic and unable to undergo colonoscopy with biopsy, 
he underwent colonoscopy as an inpatient, without any concerning 
signs of malignancy revealed. He was recommended to follow up 
with repeat colonoscopy within ___ months of discharge.

# HTN: The patient has a history of chronic HTN managed on 
carvedilol, diltiazem, and doxazosin at home. This was mostly 
well controlled while inpatient, but in the setting of high dose 
steroid administration, he developed acutely elevated BP's to 
180-190's systolic. Given self-limited nature of likely offender 
(dexamethasone), no definite changes were made to his regimen. 
He was given PRN hydralazine for his transiently elevated 
pressures, which normalized prior to discharge and cessation of 
dexamethasone therapy.

# Transaminitis: The patient had mild elevations in AST/ALT new 
between ___ and ___ in a hepatocellular pattern given normal 
bili and Alk Phos. The differential included hepatitis 
reactivation (known HBV), medication toxicity perhaps due to 
atovaquone initiation, and in the setting of transient 
hyperglycemia. Atovaquone was switched back to bactrim and HBV 
viral load was sent (pending at discharge). As the AST/ALT 
elevation was mild and stable, he was sent home with 
instructions to have LFTs rechecked as an outpatient.

# Insulin-Dependent Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: The patient has a 
history of IDDM. However, as a result of stacking insulin 
dosages in the setting of poor PO intake ___ abdominal pain and 
distention) and ___ on CKD, had significant hypoglycemia while 
in the ICU. This was managed, as above, with a d10 gtt. After 
transfer to the floor, the patient's sugars were largely in the 
150-200 range initially; but with dexamethasone therapy, he 
became increasingly hyperglycemic into the 500's, requiring 
frequent uptitration of his insulin regimen. Following cessation 
of dexamethasone therapy, his blood sugars improved drastically 
and he was discharged home on Lantus and ISS. Given that ___ 
Diabetes Team was involved closely during his ICU stay, the 
patient was instructed to follow up there for further care of 
his T2DM, especially as he will likely require further steroid 
therapy in the future.

# Perivesicular Mass/Abnormal Urine Cytology: On MRI to assess 
his abdominal pain/distention, the patient was noted to have a 
perivesicular mass. Differential for this mass included 
plasmacytoma, extramedullary hematopoiesis, or separate 
neoplasm. Given proximity of this mass to the bladder, he had 
urine cytology sent, showing atypical urothelial cells. As such, 
he was arranged for follow up with urology after discharge for 
further work-up and management of this mass.

# Acute Kidney Injury due to Pre-renal Azotemia/Chronic Kidney 
Disease: The patient presented with a baseline Cr of 1.1 as 
recently as ___. He was admitted for ___ about 2 weeks PTA 
with cast nephropathy and peak Cr >5. With treatment of his 
myeloma, his Cr improved to 2.1 on this admission, suggesting 
continued improvement. During this hospitalization, he did have 
mild ___ likely due to pre-renal azotemia i/s/o poor PO intake 
while in the ICU. There may have been an element of post-renal 
contribution as well given that he transiently required a foley. 
Throughout the rest of this admission, his Cr stabilized to 
about 1.5, likely a new baseline. He was discharged without any 
difficulty in urinating or significant electrolyte 
abnormalities.

# Obstructive Sleep Apnea; The patient has a known history of 
OSA, but was not using a CPAP at home. He was restarted on CPAP 
while in the hospital, which he tolerated well. On discharge, he 
was instructed to follow up with his PCP regarding obtaining ___ 
new CPAP machine.

CHRONIC/STABLE/RESOLVED PROBLEMS:
# Mild Pseudohemoptysis: The patient had a few days of 
small-volume hemoptysis without significant change in H&H. This 
was felt likely to be either due to low plts and 
pseudohemoptysis from either upper oropharyngeal source or 
perhaps even nasal source as patient recently had NGT placed and 
was frequently blowing his nose. This was likely also 
exacerbated by initiation of CPAP delivering dry air while 
sleeping. He was monitored clinically without any signs of 
respiratory distress and had a CXR without any acute findings. 
His symptoms rapidly self-resolved within a few days of transfer 
out of the ICU.

# Abnormal Lung Findings: The patient some audible wheezing on 
exam ___ and ___ with subjective shortness of breath. Given 
unimpressive CT torso and no history of smoking, this was felt 
to be possible atelectasis with component of aspiration 
pneumonitis while in the ICU i/s/o his active abdominal 
pain/distention and vomiting. He was given nebulizers PRN and 
clinically well appearing throughout. On discharge, his 
respiratory function was wnl.

# Dyspnea: The patient initially presented with complaint of 
dyspnea, but was found to have an O2 sat of 100% on RA. EKG, 
CXR, and exam were benign and despite concern for PE given 
underlying malignancy, the patient was not tachycardic or ever 
hypoxic. His symptoms resolved with treatment of his abdominal 
distention, suggesting dyspnea to be due to physical compression 
of his lungs due to intra-abdominal process.

# Hepatitis B: The patient has known hepatitis B, being treated 
with lamivudine therapy, which was continued this admission and 
adjusted as appropriate for renal function.

# Chronic Recurrent C. Diff: The patient was admitted amidst a 
PO vancomycin taper, which was continued as follows: 125mg PO 
QOD from ___ to ___ 125mg PO q3d for the final two weeks (last 
dose on ___. He was discharged with instructions to 
complete his taper as per this schedule.

# Depression: The patient was continued on his home duloxetine.

TECHNIQUE:  Single phase split bolus contrast: MDCT axial images were acquired
through the abdomen and pelvis following intravenous contrast administration
with split bolus technique.
Oral contrast was administered.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal radiograph ___.
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast ___

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: Visualized lungs are within normal limits. There is no evidence
of pleural or pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:
HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrates homogenous attenuation throughout. 
There is no evidence of focal lesions.  There is no evidence of intrahepatic
or extrahepatic biliary dilatation.  The gallbladder is within normal limits.

PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, without evidence of
focal lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding.

SPLEEN: The spleen shows normal size and attenuation throughout, without
evidence of focal lesions.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: The kidneys are of normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram. 
A nonobstructive, punctate calcification is present in the inferior pole of
the right kidney.  There is no evidence hydronephrosis.  There is no
perinephric abnormality.

GASTROINTESTINAL: The stomach is unremarkable.  The outer margin of the second
and third portion of the duodenum is irregular with asymmetric stranding along
the duodenum and right perirenal space.  There is colonic diverticulosis
without evidence of wall thickening and fat stranding.  The appendix is
normal.

PELVIS: There is retroperitoneal stranding in the upper pelvis, new since
prior exam.  The urinary bladder is moderately distended.  Pushing the bladder
rightward, a 5 x 4 x 2.5 cm lesion is not well characterized on this
non-contrast study. This has density slightly higher than simple fluid.  There
is no free fluid in the pelvis.

REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS: Surgical clips are noted in the prostate bed.

LYMPH NODES: There is no retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  There
is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

VASCULAR: There is no abdominal aortic aneurysm.  Mild atherosclerotic disease
is noted.

BONES:  Anterior wedge compression fracture of T12 is stable.  Again seen is
dystrophic calcification superiorly along the symphysis pubis possibly
secondary to trauma.  There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or
acute fracture.  Healed right posterior tenth and left posterior ninth rib
fractures are noted.  Degenerative changes are noted in the thoracolumbar
spine.

SOFT TISSUES:  Scarring and stranding in the left groin likely due to prior
left inguinal hernia repair.

IMPRESSION:


1. The outer margins of the second and third portions of the duodenum are
irregular with associated asymmetric stranding suggesting duodenitis. 
Recommend upper endoscopy to further evaluate the duodenum.
2. New retroperitoneal stranding in the upper pelvis may be related to
duodenitis and third spacing.
3. 5 cm lesion increased in size and more defined since prior study left of
the bladder is not well characterized on this non-contrast study.

RECOMMENDATION(S):  1.Upper endoscopy to further evaluate irregularity along
the duodenum with concern for duodenitis.
2.  MRI on 1.5 tesla to further evaluate perivesicular abnormality.

INDICATION:  History of multiple myeloma with ongoing abdominal pain,
constipation, and stranding seen around the duodenum and in the pelvis on a
CT.  Please evaluate stranding.

TECHNIQUE:  T1- and T2-weighted multiplanar images of the abdomen and pelvis
were acquired in a 1.5 T magnet.  Intravenous contrast: None.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis from ___.  CT of the
abdomen and pelvis from ___.

FINDINGS: 

Lower thorax: Within the limitations of MRI, the lung bases are clear.  The
size of the base of the heart is at the upper limits of normal.  There is no
pericardial effusion.

Liver: The liver is normal in shape and contour.  There are no morphologic
features of cirrhosis.  There is drop in signal on the in phase images in
comparison to the out of phase images, compatible with hemosiderosis.  Similar
findings are found in the spleen.  Within the limitations of this noncontrast
MRI, no focal liver lesion is identified.

Biliary: There is no intra or extrahepatic biliary duct dilation.  The
gallbladder is normal.  No stones are identified.

Pancreas: The pancreatic parenchyma is normal in signal.  There is no duct
dilation or mass.

Spleen: The spleen is normal in size, measuring 10 cm.  There are no focal
lesions.  As noted previously, there is drop in signal on the in phase images
in comparison to the out of phase images, compatible with hemosiderosis.

Adrenal Glands:  The bilateral adrenal glands are normal.

Kidneys: The kidneys are normal in size.  In the right kidney, there are two
subcentimeter cystic lesions, which are not fully characterized on this
noncontrast exam, though most likely simple cysts.  There is nonspecific
perinephric edema which is symmetric and bilateral.  There is no worrisome
renal mass or hydronephrosis.

Gastrointestinal Tract:  The stomach is normal in caliber without focal wall
thickening.  There is no gastric distention.  In the second portion of the
duodenum, there is diffuse wall thickening, wall edema, and surrounding
stranding, compatible with a duodenitis.  No discrete mass is identified, and
the focal thickening likely represents reactive wall hypertrophy.  Note, a
small mass cannot be completely excluded with certainty given the surrounding
inflammation.

The remainder of the small bowel is normal in caliber without evidence of
obstruction or focal inflammatory changes.

There is a trace amount of ascites and mesenteric edema extending inferiorly
from the area of duodenitis.  This is likely reactive to this primary
inflammatory process in the duodenum.

There is colonic diverticulosis without evidence of diverticulitis.  The large
bowel is otherwise normal without focal inflammatory changes.

Pelvis: Along the left aspect of the bladder, there is a 54 x 32 x 40 mm mass
(4, 42 and 11, 42).  It is hypointense on the T2 weighted images.  There is no
evidence of hemorrhage within the lesion.  It is incompletely characterized on
this exam.  In comparison to the prior abdominal CT from ___, this
lesion has increased in size.  At that time it contained fat.  Given the slow
growth and the fact that it contained fat in the past, this most likely is
extramedullary hematopoiesis.  The are no other masses identified in the
pelvis.  There is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.  Trace free fluid is
present, and nonspecific.

Lymph Nodes: There is no periportal, retroperitoneal, or mesenteric
lymphadenopathy.

Vasculature: The abdominal aorta is normal in caliber without evidence of an
aneurysm.  Evaluation of the vasculature is limited on this noncontrast exam.

Osseous and Soft Tissue Structures: The signal in the bone marrow is
heterogeneous, likely due to prior treatment effects.  No acute fracture is
identified.  A mild wedge compression fracture of T12 is unchanged.  There is
diffuse anasarca.  The soft tissues are otherwise unremarkable.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Duodenitis with significant surrounding inflammatory changes and
hypertrophy of the mucosa, as described above.  While no definite mass is
identified, a small one cannot be excluded with complete certainty. 
Evaluation with endoscopy after treatment is recommended.
2.  Perivesicular mass, which has been previously characterized as fat
containing.  While slightly bigger, given the presence of fat on the prior CT,
this most likely represents extramedullary hematopoiesis.  Attention on
followup exams is recommended.
3.  Hemosiderosis.
